lessons.title: Study Session 1: Turning a Skill or Body of Knowledge Into a Sellable Digital Product

blocks.text: Introduction Thandeka Nkosi has fifteen years of tailoring experience and answered the same pattern-drafting questions individually, for free, in a sewing group in Mthatha, month after month, until she tallied the hours spent typing out those explanations and realized she had already written most of a product one message at a time, never once thinking anyone would pay for what she gave away in pieces. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about the creator economy as an emerging category of expertise-based commerce. Distinguish free, scattered answers to repeated questions from a scoped, sellable digital product. Apply a method for turning a skill or body of knowledge into a sellable digital product. Recognise which of a person's skills are specific and repeatable enough to become a product. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Months of Free Answers to the Same Questions Thandeka Nkosi answered the same pattern-drafting questions individually, for free, in a sewing group, month after month, without noticing how often the questions repeated. Only when she tallied the hours spent typing out those explanations did she realize she had already written most of a product one message at a time, never once thinking anyone would pay for what she gave away in pieces. 2.2 What Research Found About the Creator Economy Renana Peres, Martin Schreier, David A. Schweidel and Alina Sorescu examined the emerging creator economy as a category of expertise-based commerce for a 2024 study. Individual creators' expertise-based activity was found to form a distinct and monetizable economic category in its own right, even though the academic study of how that expertise actually gets packaged and sold has lagged behind the practice itself. 2.3 Scoping a Skill Into a Product Finding the Question Asked Often Enough to Answer Once Noticing which specific question keeps coming back, rather than every question a person could possibly answer, narrows a whole skill set down to the one piece worth turning into a product first. Writing the Answer Once, Completely, for Everyone Writing that one answer out completely, in a form anyone asking it could use without a follow-up question, turns a habit of repeated free replies into something that can be sold the same way to the next person who asks. 2.4 Key Practices Notice which specific question keeps coming back before choosing what to turn into a product. Write the chosen answer out completely, in a form that needs no follow-up. Test the finished answer on one real person who has not asked the question before. Resist the urge to include every skill at once instead of the one worth starting with. 2.5 A Worked Example: Thandeka's First Digital Product Thandeka reviewed months of her own group messages, found that questions about adjusting a bodice block for different body shapes came up more than any other single topic, and wrote a complete, illustrated guide answering that one question fully, testing it on a seamstress who had never asked her directly before packaging it for sale. The seamstresses messaging Thandeka already trusted her enough to ask, and her answers were always exactly what they needed in the moment. Nobody had ever gathered those scattered answers into one place a new person could buy and use without waiting on a reply, and only writing the answer out completely ever turned a habit of helping into an actual product. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Answering the same question individually, for free, over and over without noticing the pattern leaves a person's most valuable knowledge scattered across messages no one else can find, exactly what happened to Thandeka for months. Trying to package an entire skill set into a first product at once, rather than the one specific question worth starting with, produces something too broad for anyone to finish or trust. 2.7 The Product Was Already There, Just Never Written Down Once Thandeka's tailoring reputation had grown for years among people who already knew to ask her directly. A newcomer with the same question had no way to reach that knowledge except by asking and waiting, and only writing the answer down once, completely, ever let that knowledge reach someone Thandeka had never actually met. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to turn a skill or body of knowledge into a sellable digital product by scoping it around the question asked most often. Study Session 2 turns from choosing what to build to structuring it so a buyer actually finishes it.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think about your own skill or area of expertise. What question do people ask you most often? 2. Write a complete answer to your most frequently asked question, in a form someone who has never met you could use without a follow-up. Practical Output: Practical Output A complete, written answer to one real, frequently asked question drawn from your own skill or expertise, scoped as the first version of a sellable digital product. 7.0 References and Further Reading Peres, R., Schreier, M., Schweidel, D.A., & Sorescu, A. (2024). The creator economy: An introduction and a call for scholarly research. International Journal of Research in Marketing, 41(3), 403 to 410. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Exodus 31:3, on being filled with the spirit of God, in wisdom, understanding and knowledge. Qur'an, Surah Al-Alaq 96:4, on the One who taught by the pen.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 2: Structuring a Digital Product So It Actually Delivers

blocks.text: Introduction Fikirte Bekele, who is Deaf, builds a mini online course on budgeting for new entrepreneurs from Debre Birhan, and packed the course with everything she knew, delivered as one long unbroken sequence of lessons with no clear stages, until only eight of her first sixty buyers ever finished it, most stalling after the second lesson with no sense of what came next. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about course length and structure and their effect on completion rates. Distinguish a digital product built as one long unbroken sequence from one structured into clear stages. Apply a method for structuring a digital product so buyers actually finish it. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Sixty Buyers, Eight Finishers Fikirte Bekele packed her budgeting course with everything she knew, delivered as one long unbroken sequence of lessons with no clear stages and no indication of how much remained at any point. Of her first sixty buyers, only eight ever finished the course, and most of the rest stalled after the second lesson with no sense of what came next or how close they were to done. 2.2 What Research Found About Course Length and Completion Katy Jordan examined completion rates across 221 massive open online courses for a 2015 study. Course length and structural design were found to measurably affect completion, with shorter courses broken into clearly signposted stages completed at far higher rates than long courses delivered as one unstructured sequence. 2.3 Structuring a Product Around Clear Stages Breaking Content Into Stages With a Visible End Point Breaking a digital product's content into a small number of clearly labeled stages, each with a visible end point, gives a buyer a sense of progress a single unbroken sequence never can. Telling the Buyer Where They Are at Every Point Telling a buyer plainly, at the start of each stage, how many remain and roughly how long each will take, replaces the guesswork of an open-ended course with a structure a buyer can actually plan around. 2.4 Key Practices Break content into a small number of clearly labeled stages with a visible end point. Tell the buyer at each stage how many remain and roughly how long each will take. Keep each individual stage short enough to finish in one sitting. 2.5 A Worked Example: Fikirte's Restructured Course Fikirte broke her budgeting course into five clearly labeled stages, each short enough to finish in one sitting, with a visible stage count and estimated time shown at the start of every stage, replacing the single unbroken sequence her first sixty buyers had struggled through. Fikirte's budgeting knowledge had never been the reason buyers stalled; every lesson she wrote was accurate and genuinely useful to a new entrepreneur. Nothing in the course told a buyer how far they had come or how far was left until she built that structure in, and only breaking the content into visible stages ever gave her buyers a reason to keep going all the way to the end. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Delivering a digital product as one long unbroken sequence, with no visible stages or sense of progress, leaves a buyer with no way to judge how much remains, exactly what stalled most of Fikirte's first sixty buyers. Making an individual stage too long to finish in one sitting undoes the benefit of structure by reintroducing the same open-ended feeling a single sequence already had. 2.7 A Buyer Finishes What Shows Them How Close They Are Fikirte's course had never lacked good information; every lesson taught something a new entrepreneur genuinely needed to know. What kept buyers from reaching that information was a structure that never showed them how far they had come, and only visible stages with a real end point ever closed that gap. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to structure a digital product into clear stages so buyers actually finish it. Study Session 3 turns from how a product is built to what it should actually cost.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think about a digital product you have made or are planning. Could a buyer tell, at any point, how much of it remains? 2. Break one real digital product's content into a small number of clearly labeled stages, each short enough to finish in one sitting. Practical Output: Practical Output A digital product outline broken into a small number of clearly labeled stages, each with a visible end point and an estimated completion time. 7.0 References and Further Reading Jordan, K. (2015). Massive open online course completion rates revisited: Assessment, length and attrition. International Review of Research in Open and Distributed Learning, 16(3). Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Luke 14:29, on laying a foundation and not being able to finish it, lest all who see it mock. Qur'an, Surah Al-Ma'idah 5:3, on this day having perfected your religion for you and completed My favour upon you.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 3: Pricing a Digital Product

blocks.text: Introduction Salimata Coulibaly sells a digital e-book collection of natural dye recipes for fabric from Bougouni, and priced it by copying a number she had seen a similar seller use, until a prospective buyer wrote in wondering aloud why the book cost twice as much as a much thinner one covering the same topic elsewhere, and Salimata realized she had no answer beyond having copied the number in the first place. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about pay-what-you-want pricing applied to digital products. Distinguish a price copied from another seller from one set against a product's own value. Apply a method for pricing a digital product deliberately. Recognise when a fixed price might be worth testing against a more flexible pricing approach. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 A Price With No Answer Behind It Salimata Coulibaly priced her natural dye recipe e-book by copying a number she had seen a similar seller use, without checking whether it reflected her own recipes' depth, what her own time developing them had cost her, or what her own audience could actually pay. A prospective buyer wrote in wondering aloud why the book cost twice as much as a much thinner one covering the same topic elsewhere, and Salimata realized she had no answer beyond having copied the number in the first place. 2.2 What Research Found About Pay-What-You-Want Pricing Ana Isabel Torres, Carlos Brito Barros and Amélia Ferreira da Silva studied pay-what-you-want pricing applied to digital products for a 2021 study. Pay-what-you-want pricing was found to produce greater total revenue than a fixed price in some cases, through a larger number of transactions offsetting lower amounts paid per transaction, evidence that price is a deliberate lever rather than a fixed given. 2.3 Pricing a Product Deliberately Calculating What the Product Actually Cost to Create Calculating the real time and any direct cost that went into creating a digital product, rather than skipping straight to a number that sounds reasonable, gives a price an actual floor to be measured against. Checking a Price Against the Product's Own Depth, Not a Competitor's Comparing a price against what the product itself actually delivers, depth, length, uniqueness, rather than against a number seen on someone else's page, keeps a price tied to the product a buyer will actually receive. 2.4 Key Practices Calculate the real time and cost that went into creating the product before setting a price. Check a price against the product's own depth and length, not a competitor's number. Consider testing a flexible pricing approach if a fixed price has not been validated with real buyers. Revisit a price once real sales data shows how buyers are actually responding to it. 2.5 A Worked Example: Salimata's Recalculated Price Salimata calculated the actual hours she had spent developing and testing her dye recipes, set a price that reflected both that time and the book's genuine depth compared to thinner alternatives, and could finally explain exactly what a buyer's payment covered when asked. Salimata's dye recipes themselves had taken real time and real trial to perfect; every recipe in the book had been tested and refined through actual use. The price attached to that book had come from someone else's page rather than from her own costs or her own product's depth, and only calculating her price from scratch ever gave her an answer she could actually explain to a customer. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Copying a competitor's price without checking it against a product's own depth or cost leaves a seller unable to explain their own number, exactly the position Salimata found herself in. Assuming a fixed price is the only option, without ever testing a more flexible approach, can leave real revenue on the table that a different pricing model might have captured. 2.7 A Price Should Be an Answer, Not a Guess Salimata's recipes carried real value earned through actual testing, value that had never once been reflected in a price borrowed from someone else's book. Only calculating a price from her own costs and her own product's depth ever gave that price an answer behind it, rather than a guess she could not defend. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to price a digital product deliberately, against its own cost and depth rather than a competitor's number. Study Session 4 turns from what a product costs to how quickly and smoothly it actually reaches the buyer who paid for it.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think about how you currently price, or would price, a digital product. Is the number based on your own costs and depth, or borrowed from somewhere else? 2. Calculate the real time and cost behind one real digital product, and set a price you could explain to a customer who asked about it. Practical Output: Practical Output A price calculation for one real digital product, based on actual time and cost invested and the product's own depth, with a short explanation a customer could be given if asked. 7.0 References and Further Reading Torres, A.I., Barros, C.L., & da Silva, A.F. (2021). The pay what you want pricing strategy applied to digital products: An essay. Journal of Revenue and Pricing Management. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Proverbs 31:18, on perceiving that her merchandise is good. Qur'an, Surah Ash-Shu'ara 26:182, on weighing with an even balance.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 4: Packaging and Automating Digital Delivery

blocks.text: Introduction Ayanda Zulu sells digital financial planner templates from Vryheid, and manually emailed each file to a buyer only after checking payment notifications by hand, until a weekend promotion brought a rush of orders large enough that twenty buyers waited up to two days for a product they had paid for instantly, several messaging to ask whether they had been scammed. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about good and bad friction in customer experience. Distinguish delivery friction that frustrates a buyer from delay that does not actually harm the experience. Apply a method for packaging and automating digital delivery. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Paid Instantly, Waited Two Days Ayanda Zulu manually emailed each planner template to a buyer only after checking her payment notifications by hand, a system that worked without incident while her sales stayed low. A weekend promotion brought a rush of orders large enough that twenty buyers waited up to two days for a product they had paid for instantly, and several messaged asking whether they had been scammed. 2.2 What Research Found About Good and Bad Friction Manjunath Padigar, Yi Li and Chandana N. Manjunath examined different types of friction in customer experience for a 2025 study. Friction that frustrated a customer's actual goal, such as an unnecessary delay between payment and delivery, was found to damage the customer experience, while other kinds of friction did not carry the same cost, meaning delay itself is not neutral when it blocks the very thing a customer just paid for. 2.3 Automating the Handoff From Payment to Delivery Connecting Payment Confirmation Directly to File Delivery Setting up a system where a confirmed payment automatically triggers delivery of the file, rather than waiting for a person to notice and act on a notification, removes the exact point where a busy period turns a paid order into a wait. Testing the Automated Handoff Before It Is Needed Testing the automated delivery system with a real purchase before a high-volume period arrives, rather than trusting it untested, catches a broken link or missing file while the cost of finding out is still low. 2.4 Key Practices Set up automatic delivery triggered directly by a confirmed payment. Test the automated delivery system with a real purchase before a high-volume period arrives. Keep a manual backup process ready in case the automated system fails. 2.5 A Worked Example: Ayanda's Automated Delivery Ayanda connected her payment platform to an automatic delivery system that sent the correct file the moment a payment was confirmed, tested it herself with a real purchase before her next promotion, and kept a simple manual process ready in case anything failed. Ayanda's planner templates had earned real trust among the buyers who received them promptly before that weekend; the templates themselves gave no one reason to doubt her. The gap between a confirmed payment and an actual file reaching a buyer had depended entirely on Ayanda noticing a notification in time, and only automating that handoff ever closed the gap a busy weekend had exposed. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Relying on a person to manually notice a payment and send a file, rather than an automatic system, works only until volume outpaces attention, exactly what happened to Ayanda's weekend promotion. Trusting an automated delivery system without testing it first risks discovering a broken link only after a real customer has already paid and is waiting. 2.7 The Wait a Customer Never Expected Costs More Than the Delay Itself Ayanda's templates were complete and genuinely useful to everyone who eventually received one that weekend. A payment confirmed instantly had never guaranteed a file would follow just as fast, and only automating that handoff ever made the two match the way a buyer had every reason to expect. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to package and automate digital delivery so a confirmed payment reaches the buyer without unnecessary delay. Study Session 5 turns from delivering the product to writing the sales page that convinces someone to buy it in the first place.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think about your own delivery process, or one you are planning. Does a confirmed payment lead straight to delivery, or does it depend on someone noticing? 2. Set up or describe an automated delivery step for one real digital product, and test it with a real or simulated purchase. Practical Output: Practical Output A tested automated delivery process for one real digital product, triggered directly by payment confirmation, with a manual backup plan described. 7.0 References and Further Reading Padigar, M., Li, Y., & Manjunath, C.N. (2025). "Good" and "bad" frictions in customer experience: Conceptual foundations and implications. Psychology & Marketing, 42(1), 21 to 43. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Proverbs 3:27, on not withholding good from those to whom it is due, when it is in the power of thine hand to do it. Qur'an, Surah Al-Baqarah 2:185, on Allah intending ease and not intending hardship.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 5: Writing a Digital Product Sales Page That Converts

blocks.text: Introduction Rahel Girma, who has run her home-based catering business alone since her husband's passing, sells a video course on catering from her own kitchen in Debre Markos, and built a sales page that was a plain bullet list of topics with no image and no headline speaking to a visitor's actual situation, until a friend who had taken the course looked at the page and told Rahel she would never have guessed its quality from reading it. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about the elements of landing page design that drive conversion. Distinguish a sales page listing features from one built around the elements shown to convert. Apply a method for writing a digital product sales page that converts. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 A Page That Undersold What It Was Selling Rahel's sales page for her home-based catering course was a plain bullet list of topics covered, with no image, no headline speaking to a visitor's actual situation, and nothing that suggested what the course could genuinely do for someone. A friend who had taken the course and knew firsthand how good it was looked at the page and told Rahel she would never have guessed its quality from reading it. 2.2 What Research Found About Landing Page Design and Conversion Marcin Hylewski, Artur Pluskota and Błażej Abel analyzed over twenty-five thousand landing pages for a 2025 study of design and structure. The headline, hero image, primary call-to-action and form design were found to account for most of the difference in conversion rate between pages, well ahead of other design elements tested. 2.3 Building a Sales Page Around What Converts Writing a Headline That Names the Visitor's Actual Problem Writing a headline that names the specific problem a visitor already has, rather than simply describing the product, gives that visitor an immediate reason to believe the page was written for them. Pairing the Headline With an Image and One Clear Action Pairing that headline with a genuine image of the product or its result, and a single, clearly visible action for the visitor to take next, keeps the page from asking a visitor to work out what to do on their own. 2.4 Key Practices Write a headline that names the visitor's actual problem, not just the product's topic. Pair the headline with a genuine image and one clear, visible call to action. Keep the page focused on one product and one action, not several competing options. 2.5 A Worked Example: Rahel's Rebuilt Sales Page Rahel rewrote her headline around the exact worry keeping a visitor from booking her course, catering a first paying event without losing money on ingredients, added a real photo from one of her own catered events, and placed a single clear button leading straight to purchase. Rahel's course had already proven itself to every student who actually watched it, including the friend who praised it so directly. A stranger arriving at the sales page had no way to feel that same quality from a bare list of topics, and only a headline and image built around a real problem ever gave that stranger a reason to believe the course was worth what it actually delivered. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Listing a product's topics without a headline that names a visitor's actual problem leaves a sales page describing the product instead of speaking to the person reading it, exactly what undersold Rahel's course. Offering a visitor several possible actions instead of one clear one asks them to make a decision the page itself should have already made simpler. 2.7 A Sales Page Should Feel Written for the Person Reading It Every student who actually sat through Rahel's course left knowing more than they arrived with, exactly as the friend who praised it could confirm firsthand. The sales page describing that course to a stranger had given that stranger no way to sense any of it, and only rebuilding the page around a real problem and a real image ever let a new visitor feel what an existing student already knew. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to write a digital product sales page built around the headline, image and call to action shown to convert. Study Session 6 closes this course by turning to how a digital product is protected once it starts selling.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think about a sales page you have written, or would write. Does the headline name a real problem, or just describe the product? 2. Rewrite the headline for one real digital product's sales page so it names the specific problem the product solves. Practical Output: Practical Output A rewritten headline, paired with a description of the image and single call to action to use, for one real digital product's sales page. 7.0 References and Further Reading Hylewski, M., Pluskota, A., & Abel, B. (2025). The effect of landing page design and structure on conversion rates. Applied Marketing Analytics, 10(4), 324 to 335. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Proverbs 16:21, on the sweetness of the lips increasing learning. Qur'an, Surah Fussilat 41:33, on who is better in speech than one who invites to Allah.

lessons.title: Study Session 6: Protecting a Digital Product While Keeping It Accessible

blocks.text: Introduction Adaeze Obi sells a digital course on small business record keeping from Okigwe, and after discovering her course files being resold on an unrelated page, locked her files behind multiple passwords, obscuring watermarks and a viewing limit that expired after a single access, until the restrictions generated more support complaints from honest, paying customers than the original piracy had ever cost her directly. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about the trade-off between digital protection and legitimate access. Distinguish protection that deters unauthorized sharing from protection that punishes a paying customer. Apply a method for protecting a digital product while keeping it genuinely accessible. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Locked So Tight Even Paying Customers Couldn't Get In After discovering her small business record-keeping course being resold on an unrelated page, Adaeze Obi locked her course files behind multiple passwords, watermarks that obscured the content, and a viewing limit that expired after a single access. The restrictions generated more support complaints from honest, paying customers locked out of their own purchase than the original piracy had ever cost her directly. 2.2 What Research Found About the Trade-Off Between Protection and Access Arun Sundararajan examined the trade-off between digital protection and legitimate customer access for a 2004 study. Heavier technical protection was found to reduce piracy but also to make the legitimate product less attractive to paying customers, meaning protection carries a real cost to the honest buyer and not only to the person attempting to copy the product. 2.3 Protecting a Product Without Punishing the Buyer Choosing Protection That Targets Sharing, Not Ordinary Use Choosing a protection method that specifically targets unauthorized redistribution, such as a personalized watermark tied to the buyer, rather than one that restricts an honest buyer's ordinary use, such as an expiring link, keeps protection aimed at the actual problem. Weighing How Much Protection the Product Genuinely Needs Weighing how much protection a specific product genuinely needs against how much friction that protection adds to a paying customer's experience, rather than applying the heaviest available option by default, keeps the response proportional to the actual risk. 2.4 Key Practices Choose protection that targets unauthorized redistribution rather than an honest buyer's ordinary use. Weigh how much protection a specific product genuinely needs against the friction it adds. Watch support complaints for signs that protection is affecting paying customers, not just pirates. 2.5 A Worked Example: Adaeze's Rebalanced Protection Adaeze replaced her expiring single-view files and obscuring watermark with a personalized watermark carrying each buyer's own name and order number, removed the viewing limit entirely, and kept ordinary access simple for anyone who had actually paid. Adaeze's record-keeping course had nothing to do with why it ended up resold elsewhere; the piracy reflected nothing about the course's own quality or content. The protection she added afterward had punished her honest buyers far more reliably than it had ever stopped the person reselling her files, and only replacing that protection with something aimed specifically at sharing ever let a paying customer reach what they had bought without friction. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Applying the heaviest available protection by default, without weighing it against a specific product's actual risk, punishes honest buyers more reliably than it stops determined piracy, exactly what happened to Adaeze's locked-down course. Ignoring a rise in support complaints after adding new protection misses the clearest signal that the restriction has started harming paying customers instead of pirates. 2.7 Protection Aimed at Everyone Protects the Product From No One in Particular Adaeze's course content stayed identical in quality between the version that got pirated and the version locked down afterward. What changed was how much friction a genuine buyer had to fight through to reach content already paid for, and only aiming protection specifically at sharing, rather than at every user equally, ever gave paying customers back the access they were owed. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to protect a digital product from unauthorized sharing without punishing the customers who paid for it. This closes Course 101 and prepares you for Course 102, Online Course Creation and Cohort-Based Learning, the next course in Pathway 64.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think about any protection you use, or would use, on a digital product. Does it target sharing specifically, or does it also burden a genuine buyer? 2. Review or design a protection approach for one real digital product that targets unauthorized sharing without restricting an honest buyer's ordinary access. Practical Output: Practical Output A protection plan for one real digital product that specifically targets unauthorized redistribution while keeping ordinary access simple for a paying customer. 7.0 References and Further Reading Sundararajan, A. (2004). Managing digital piracy: Pricing and protection. Information Systems Research, 15(3), 287 to 308. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: 1 Samuel 17:34, on going out after the lion and the bear to rescue what had been taken from the flock. Qur'an, Surah Al-Hijr 15:9, on having sent down the message, and indeed being its guardian.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

quiz.q: Twenty buyers waited up to two days for a product they had paid for instantly, and several asked if they had been scammed. What did this reveal?
options: Ayanda's planner templates had stopped being useful to buyers
Relying on a person to manually notice a payment and send a file works only until volume outpaces attention
Digital planner templates should not be sold online
Ayanda had been overpricing her templates
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Packaging and Automating Digital Delivery) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Padigar, Li and Manjunath's 2025 study, what kind of friction was found to damage customer experience?
options: Friction that frustrates a customer's actual goal, such as an unnecessary delay between payment and delivery
All friction, regardless of type
Only friction related to price, not delivery
No type of friction was found to matter
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Packaging and Automating Digital Delivery) before continuing.

quiz.q: What does this session recommend connecting directly to file delivery?
options: A weekly manual review of all orders
Confirmed payment, so delivery triggers automatically
A customer's social media activity
Nothing; delivery should always be handled manually
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Packaging and Automating Digital Delivery) before continuing.

quiz.q: A friend who had taken Rahel's course said she would never have guessed its quality from the sales page. What did this reveal?
options: Rahel's catering course had stopped teaching anything useful
A sales page listing topics without a headline naming a visitor's actual problem describes the product instead of speaking to the reader
Video courses about catering cannot be sold online
Rahel had been pricing her course too high
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 5 (Writing a Digital Product Sales Page That Converts) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Hylewski, Pluskota and Abel's 2025 study of over 25,000 landing pages, which elements accounted for most of the difference in conversion rate?
options: The headline, hero image, primary call-to-action and form design
Only the total word count of the page
The color of the page background alone
The number of testimonials included, regardless of other design
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 5 (Writing a Digital Product Sales Page That Converts) before continuing.

quiz.q: What does this session recommend a headline name?
options: The product's full list of features
The visitor's actual problem, not just the product's topic
The seller's personal biography
The price of the product alone
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 5 (Writing a Digital Product Sales Page That Converts) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: Thandeka had already written most of a product for free, one message at a time, without realizing it. What did this reveal?
options: Thandeka's tailoring skill had stopped being valuable to other seamstresses
Answering the same question repeatedly, for free, without noticing the pattern, leaves valuable knowledge scattered where no one else can find it
Pattern drafting cannot be taught through a digital product
Thandeka had been undercharging for her tailoring services
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Turning a Skill or Body of Knowledge Into a Sellable Digital Product) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: According to Peres, Schreier, Schweidel and Sorescu's 2024 study, what was found about individual creators' expertise-based activity?
options: It forms a distinct and monetizable economic category in its own right
It cannot be measured or studied academically
It only applies to creators on video platforms
It has no relationship to traditional entrepreneurship
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Turning a Skill or Body of Knowledge Into a Sellable Digital Product) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: What does this session recommend looking for when choosing what to turn into a first digital product?
options: Every skill a person has, combined into one product
The specific question that keeps coming back most often
Whatever a competitor is already selling
The most complicated topic a person knows
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Turning a Skill or Body of Knowledge Into a Sellable Digital Product) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: Only eight of Fikirte's first sixty buyers finished her budgeting course. What did this reveal?
options: Fikirte's budgeting knowledge had stopped being accurate
Delivering a course as one long unbroken sequence, with no visible stages, leaves a buyer with no way to judge how much remains
Budgeting cannot be taught through a digital course
Fikirte had been charging too much for the course
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Structuring a Digital Product So It Actually Delivers) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: According to Jordan's 2015 study of 221 massive open online courses, what was found to affect completion rates?
options: Course length and structural design
Only the price charged for the course
The time of year the course launched
The number of buyers alone, regardless of structure
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Structuring a Digital Product So It Actually Delivers) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: What does this session recommend telling a buyer at the start of each stage?
options: Nothing; buyers should discover the structure on their own
How many stages remain and roughly how long each will take
Only the total price already paid
The names of other buyers who finished
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Structuring a Digital Product So It Actually Delivers) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: A customer asked Salimata why her book cost twice as much as a thinner one on the same topic, and she had no answer. What did this reveal?
options: Salimata's dye recipes had stopped being useful to customers
Copying a competitor's price without checking it against a product's own depth or cost leaves a seller unable to explain their own number
Digital recipe collections should not be priced at all
Salimata had been undercharging for her recipes
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 3 (Pricing a Digital Product) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: According to Torres, Barros and da Silva's 2021 study, what was found about pay-what-you-want pricing compared to a fixed price?
options: It produced greater total revenue in some cases, through more transactions offsetting lower amounts paid per transaction
It always produced less revenue than a fixed price
It had no measurable effect on revenue
It only worked for physical products, not digital ones
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 3 (Pricing a Digital Product) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: What does this session recommend calculating before setting a price?
options: Nothing; a price should simply match a competitor's
The real time and cost that went into creating the product
Only the price of the cheapest similar product available
The buyer's total household income
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 3 (Pricing a Digital Product) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: Twenty buyers waited up to two days for a product they had paid for instantly, and several asked if they had been scammed. What did this reveal?
options: Ayanda's planner templates had stopped being useful to buyers
Relying on a person to manually notice a payment and send a file works only until volume outpaces attention
Digital planner templates should not be sold online
Ayanda had been overpricing her templates
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Packaging and Automating Digital Delivery) before continuing.
